newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria's Zeroual seen gaining in war on Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's Zeroual seen gaining in war on Islamists.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual is gaining ground in his battle to crush an Islamist insurgency against his military-dominated rule but faces tough choices on his oil-producing nation's future, European analysts say.

If confirmed, the killing of Antar Zouabri, the feared leader of the rebel Armed Islamic Group (GIA), in a military operation this week would be a symbolic success against one of the most ruthless figures to emerge in more than five years of civil conflict in which an estimated 60,000 people have died.
A source close to the Algerian security services said Zouabri, 27, and many of his followers were killed in an ambush last Tuesday. Algerian newspapers said up to 140 were wiped out.
But the radio station Medi-1, broadcasting from the north Moroccan city of Tangier, said it had received a statement from the GIA denying reports that Zouabri had been killed.

In any case the GIA, blamed by the authorities for dozens of massacres and attacks on foreigners, has thrown up new and ever more fearsome leaders each time its chief has been eliminated, and it is not the biggest Islamic guerrilla group.
Nor have such military successes stopped the slaughter, both in outlying villages and towns and in bomb attacks and assassinations in Algiers.

European experts say the real choice facing Zeroual and the handful of fellow generals who run Algeria is what to do about the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) political party and its guerrilla wing, the Islamic Salvation Army (AIS).

"The killing of Zouabri would not be fundamentally very important. The political key is what they do about the FIS in the coming months, whether they reintegrate it into the political landscape or not," said historian Benjamin Stora, one of France's leading Algeria-watchers.
The AIS is strong in eastern Algeria and in some parts of the west, as well as the centre, while the GIA is largely concentrated in the Algiers area and the plains and hills south of the capital.

Zeroual scored points when he freed the historic leader of the FIS, Abassi Madani, jailed since 1991, on parole on July 15, a week after releasing the banned movement's chief spokesman Abdelkader Hachani. But the party's hardline number two, Ali Belhaj, remains imprisoned.

The president, who diplomats said appears to have won a freer hand from his military colleagues, has thus coupled the military crackdown on the most hardline Islamic rebels with conciliatory gestures towards more moerate Islamist politicians.
Since being released, Madani has suggested that the FIS could be willing to call a truce. He was immediately warned by the authorities to stop making political statements.

His conditional release nevertheless raised the possibility that Zeroual would eventually allow credible Islamist leaders to play a political role, after allowing two other officially sanctioned Islamist parties to contest a parliamentary election last month.

The president also announced this week the final stage of a controlled return to a facade of democracy by calling municipal elections for October 23, following last month's legislative poll from which the FIS was excluded.

The legal opposition parties, which protested at alleged widespread electoral fraud in the parliamentary voting, are negotiating with the government on conditions for participating in the local elections.

Diplomats said Zeroual may use both the municipal elections and an easing of the ban on the political wing of the FIS as pawns in his strategy for winning greater outside financial assistance and investment in Algeria.
Algiers is negotiating a new trade and aid agreement with the European Union which will include a human rights clause, and such gestures could help ease the way.

More crucially, the diplomats said the authorities would want to show some goodwill on moves towards a political opening to win favourable terms from the International Monetary Fund and foreign creditors in negotiations on its $40 billion debt.
